new_statements.quote: The following is the maximal projection of Chung syllable structure. However, some Chung words have a sesqui-syllabic structure (Matisoff 1973), initiated with an unstressed minor syllable, of CV structure, followed by a stressed, major syllable, which has either a CVC, CVV, CCVV, or a CCVVC structure. [...] Sesqui-syllabic Words. These are a type of disyllabic words where main, stressed syllables are preceded by minor, unstressed pre-syllables. The vowel of the pre-syllable is usually written as the neutralized vowel [ə].

new_statements.rule_in_words: Sa'och (Chung) is non-tonal with four phonation registers; native words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables, and stress falls on the major (main) syllable, i.e. the final syllable; any preceding minor syllable (CV with a neutralized vowel [ə]) is unstressed and carries no register contrast. Stress is thus predictable (non-contrastive), always on the word-final full syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Related remarks: 'There is no register contrast in minor, or unstressed, syllables' (p. 50); 'There are no occurrences of short vowels in open stressed syllables' (p. 49); the pre-syllable vowel is neutralized to [ə]; Chung Yuy tends to simplify or drop the pre-syllable altogether (pp. 62-63, 94-95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: phonological description of the Chung (Sa'och) word in citation forms; the thesis covers both Chung Yuy (Thung Na village, Kanchanaburi, Thailand) and Chung Yul (Veal Renh, Prey Nob district, Kampong Som, Cambodia). Statement is about monosyllables and sesqui-syllables (the only native word shapes described; polysyllabic loans from Thai/Khmer are not treated for stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Isara 2007 calls the language 'Chung' (autonym [tɕʰṳˀŋ]); 'Saoch' is the Khmer exonym. The thesis describes both varieties of saoc1239: Chung Yuy (Thung Na village, Kanchanaburi, Thailand; descendants of 1830s war captives) and Chung Yul (Veal Renh, Prey Nob district, Kampong Som / Preah Sihanouk, Cambodia); the syllable/stress statement is given for 'Chung' generally, with the varieties differing only in pre-syllable complexity (Chung Yuy simplifies or drops the pre-syllable). Glottolog lists no dialect children under saoc1239. The Headley 1985 statement is genus-level (Pearic) but explicitly includes 'Saoch of Veal Renh' among its dialects.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Chung phonological inventories' pp. 72-74: 21 consonants, 9 short + 9 long vowels ('There are no occurrences of short vowels in open stressed syllables', p. 73), 'Chung is a non-tonal language' with 4 registers (p. 73); sec. 3.2 pre-syllables pp. 74-75 (CY has /ka-/ pre-syllable almost everywhere, CL more varied). No explicit stress-placement sentence; condensed from the 2007 thesis.
